title: Nobody expected tears from the Son of God.
paragraphs: Nobody expected tears from the Son of God.

Not there.
Not in that moment.
Not standing inches away from the miracle He already knew He was about to perform.

Because Jesus was not confused.
He was not powerless.
He was not uncertain.
He already told His disciples:
“This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God…” — John 11:4
He already knew Lazarus would rise.
And yet…
He wept.

Two words in English.
But beneath those words lives one of the deepest revelations in all of Scripture.

“Jesus wept.”
— John 11:35
In Greek:

ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
edákrysen ho Iēsoûs

The word used here is:
ἐδάκρυσεν (edákrysen)

This is not loud wailing.
Not theatrical mourning.
Not emotional collapse.

It means:
to shed tears silently…
to weep deeply…
to cry from inward pain.
This matters because a different Greek word was used for the crowd around Him.
John 11:33 says the mourners were:
κλαίω (klaiō)

Meaning:
loud lamentation,
public grieving,
audible sobbing.
But Jesus did not mourn like the crowd.
He carried something heavier.

The Son of God stood in front of a tomb He was seconds away from emptying…
and still cried.
Why?
Because this moment was never only about Lazarus.
Jesus was staring directly at everything sin had done to humanity.

The tomb.
The funeral.
The broken sisters.
The grief.
The unbelief.
The fear.
The sting of death.
He was face to face with the curse Eden unleashed into the world.
Many people think Jesus cried because Lazarus died.
But Jesus already knew death would lose in a few moments.
What shattered Him was what death had become to humanity.
This is why the next verse becomes extremely important.
John 11:33 says:
“He groaned in the spirit, and was troubled.”
The Greek here is astonishing.

ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι
enebrímēsato tō pneumati
This word does not merely mean sadness.

It carries the idea of:
deep indignation,
outrage,
agitation,
even a restrained fury.
Ancient Greek usage often connected this word to the snorting of a war horse preparing for battle.
Jesus was not simply emotional.
He was furious at death itself.

The grave standing before Him was an enemy.
A thief.
An intruder.
Because death was never part of God’s original design.
In Hebrew thought, death is the visible evidence of humanity’s separation from God caused by sin.
Genesis warned:

“For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”
— Genesis 3:19
And now Jesus — God wrapped in flesh — stands before the physical manifestation of humanity’s curse.
And He trembles.

Not in weakness.
In confrontation.
This was not merely a funeral scene.
This was a declaration of war.

The tears of Christ were not helpless tears.
They were the tears of a Savior preparing to crush the thing destroying His children.
That changes everything.
Because many believers secretly think God watches suffering emotionally detached.
But Lazarus’ tomb destroys that lie forever.

Jesus knew resurrection was coming…
and still entered their pain fully.

He did not say:
“Stop crying.”
“Get over it.”
“You should have more faith.”
Instead…
He stepped into their grief.
This is why Hebrews says:

“For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses…”
— Hebrews 4:15
The Greek word for sympathize:
συμπαθῆσαι (sympathēsai)

Literally means:
to suffer alongside.
Jesus does not observe human pain from a distance.
He enters it.

That means every believer who has cried alone…
every exhausted mother…
every grieving father…
every depressed teenager…
every person silently fighting anxiety…
every believer wondering if heaven sees them…
needs to understand something:
The God of Scripture is not emotionally absent.
Christ weeps with His people.
But there is another layer almost nobody talks about.
When Jesus arrives, Martha says:

“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.”
— John 11:21
Mary later says the exact same thing.

This reveals something heartbreaking:
they believed Jesus could prevent death…
but not reverse it.
Their faith had limits.

And honestly?
So does ours sometimes.

We believe God can help before things collapse.
But once the tomb closes…
once the marriage dies…
once the addiction wins…
once the child walks away…
once hope disappears…
we assume it’s over.
But Lazarus’ tomb was specifically chosen to destroy hopeless theology.
By the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days.

In Jewish understanding, many believed the spirit lingered near the body for three days.
Day four meant complete finality.

Impossible.
Irreversible.
Hopeless.
And that was exactly when Jesus chose to arrive.
Because Christ specializes in entering situations humanity has already buried.
Some of you reading this have sealed things emotionally in a tomb.

Dreams.
Purity.
Faith.
Joy.
Calling.
Marriage.
Identity.
Hope.
But the voice that cried outside Lazarus’ grave still speaks.
In Greek, Jesus shouted:

Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω
Lázare, deûro éxō

“Lazarus, come out!”
— John 11:43
And death obeyed Him.
Do you realize what this means?

The same Christ who wept…
also conquered the thing causing the tears.
That is the Gospel.
Not a distant God giving motivational speeches from heaven.

But God entering death personally…
then defeating it from the inside.
And Lazarus’ tomb was only the preview.

Because soon…
Jesus Himself would enter another tomb.
And this time there would be no miracle after four days from outside the grave.

He Himself would carry humanity’s sin,
humanity’s curse,
humanity’s punishment,
humanity’s death.
Isaiah 53 says:
“Surely He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows…”
The Hebrew word for griefs:
חֳלִי (choli)

Can mean:
sickness,
suffering,
affliction,
pain.
He carried all of it.
And three days later…
the tomb lost again.
This is why Jesus weeping matters so much.

Because His tears prove His love.
And His resurrection proves His authority.
He is not merely compassionate enough to cry with humanity.
He is powerful enough to save humanity.
Somebody reading this has been questioning whether God still sees your pain.
Lazarus’ tomb is your answer.

Christ still steps toward graves.
Christ still calls dead things out.
Christ still enters impossible situations.
Christ still weeps with broken people.
Christ still defeats darkness.
And one day, according to Revelation 21:4:
“He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. There shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying…”

The One who once wept beside humanity…
will personally end the reason humanity weeps.
That promise is still alive.
The tomb was never the end of the story… it was where Heaven began rewriting it.
